abstracts.abstract: The growing carbon footprint of data centers necessitates a fundamental shift in how we model and optimize computing resources. This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework for carbon-aware computing that integrates dynamic carbon intensity modeling with workload scheduling theory. Unlike conventional green computing approaches that optimize purely on energy consumption, our framework explicitly accounts for the temporal and spatial variability of grid carbon intensity. We formulate the carbon-aware scheduling problem as a Markov decision process and derive optimal policies under various carbon intensity scenarios. A key theoretical contribution is the establishment of the Carbon-Aware Computation Equivalence Principle, which characterizes the fundamental trade-off between computational delay and carbon emissions. We prove that any optimal carbon-aware schedule must satisfy this principle and provide necessary conditions for its satisfaction. Rigorous analysis on real carbon intensity data from three major grid regions demonstrates that our framework achieves 40% greater carbon reduction compared to state-of-the-art energy-efficient algorithms while maintaining Quality of Service (QoS) requirements. This work establishes the theoretical foundation for a new computing paradigm that treats carbon awareness as a first-class optimization objective, thereby contributing to sustainable computing research with significant implications for computing for sustainability applications.

Energy-efficient computing in large-scale distributed systems requires sophisticated resource allocation strategies that account for heterogeneous workloads and varying power profiles. This paper presents an enhanced theoretical analysis of power-aware task scheduling with substantial improvements over existing models. We extend the classical makespan minimization framework by incorporating power consumption characteristics, thermal constraints, and renewable energy availability into a unified optimization model. The proposed Multi-Objective Power-Aware Scheduling (MOPAS) theory provides closed-form bounds on the achievable trade-offs between energy consumption, completion time, and thermal reliability. We prove that MOPAS achieves (1 + ε)-approximation for any ε > 0 with polynomial-time complexity, significantly improving upon the previously known logarithmic approximation ratios. Furthermore, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for schedule feasibility under peak power constraints, a theoretical result that has been missing in the literature. Extensive trace-driven simulations using Google cluster data demonstrate that our theoretically-grounded algorithm reduces energy costs by 27% compared to best-known heuristics while maintaining thermal safety margins. This theoretical advancement provides practitioners with provably efficient algorithms for designing sustainable data centers and low-power systems with guaranteed performance bounds.

The advent of renewable energy-powered computing demands a paradigm shift in system architecture for sustainable data centers. This paper presents CarbonSense, a groundbreaking carbon-aware container orchestration platform that fundamentally reimagines workload management in green cloud computing environments. CarbonSense introduces three novel system components: (1) a real-time carbon intensity monitoring API that interfaces with regional grid operators, (2) an ML-based carbon forecasting engine that predicts intensity fluctuations up to 24 hours ahead, and (3) a carbon-aware scheduler that jointly optimizes workload placement, migration, and deferral decisions. The system architecture implements a hierarchical control plane that enables fine-grained carbon-aware decisions at the container level while maintaining global optimization objectives. We deployed CarbonSense on a production-scale Kubernetes cluster powered by 40% renewable energy and conducted extensive evaluations over a three-month period. Results demonstrate that CarbonSense achieves 35% higher renewable energy utilization compared to conventional energy-aware systems while reducing cumulative carbon emissions by 28%. Notably, the forecasting engine achieves 94% prediction accuracy, enabling proactive workload scheduling. This work introduces a new system design philosophy for sustainable computing where carbon awareness is embedded into the core orchestration layer.

Energy monitoring and optimization in sustainable computing environments face significant challenges due to the heterogeneity of hardware components and the complexity of modern workloads. This paper presents EcoMon, an enhanced energy monitoring and optimization framework for green data centers that substantially improves upon existing approaches through several key innovations. EcoMon implements an edge-cloud collaborative architecture where lightweight monitoring agents are deployed on individual servers while a centralized optimization engine performs global energy-aware resource management. The system introduces adaptive sampling techniques that dynamically adjust monitoring frequency based on workload characteristics, reducing communication overhead by 60% without sacrificing accuracy. We developed novel power models that capture the complex relationship between CPU utilization, memory access patterns, and energy consumption for heterogeneous processor architectures. The optimization engine employs a two-stage approach: offline planning using integer linear programming and online adaptation using reinforcement learning to handle workload variability. We evaluated EcoMon on a 64-server cluster running production workloads for six months. The system achieved 31% energy reduction compared to the baseline while maintaining 98.6% task completion rate. Hardware sustainability is enhanced through reduced thermal throttling events, extending server lifetime by an estimated 15%. EcoMon provides a practical and scalable solution for energy-efficient resource management in sustainable data centers.
